title: Khadijah dies
hookLine: Khadijah dies, and in Bukhari's reports he never stops speaking of her

cards: In Medina, years after the events we're following, a sheep has been slaughtered in the Prophet's household. He cuts it into portions and sends some out, not to his companions, but to a few women around the city.
Aisha, his wife, watches this happen again and again. Who are they? The friends of a woman she never met.
The boycott is over, and a new part of the story opens, the part of sorrow, with a loss he carried for the rest of his life. Today: Khadijah dies.

teach.h: THE ONE HE RAN HOME TO.
teach.b: Khadijah was the one he ran home to when the revelation began, the one who wrapped him up and said that God would never disgrace him.

She was his wife and his shelter, and, as the sirah tells it, she stood beside him through the hungry years in the valley. Then, after the boycott, she dies. The sources are short about the death itself.
What they keep, at length, is what came after.
Aisha, in Sahih al-Bukhari, is frank about it: she was never jealous of any woman the way she was of Khadijah, though she had never seen her, because the Prophet mentioned her so often.
The sheep and the portions for Khadijah's friends come from the same report. Another report in Bukhari is smaller still.
Khadijah's sister, Hala, comes to the door and asks permission to come in, and something in the way she asks is like Khadijah. He is shaken by it, and calls out, O Allah, Hala.

teach.h: A SISTER'S VOICE AT THE DOOR.
teach.b: Years after her death, a voice at the door could still do that.

teach.h: HER LOVE WAS GIVEN TO HIM.
teach.b: In Sahih Muslim he puts it in his own words: he was given her love. Not chosen, not earned. Given.
And Bukhari reports that Jibril told him to give Khadijah good news of a house in Paradise, with no noise in it and no tiredness. The grief is real. The love is called a gift.
And the memory shows up in ordinary things: meat for her friends, a sister's knock.

how: Muslims honor Khadijah as a Mother of the Believers; her life and the Prophet's love for her are retold in sirah study, and Muslims pray for mercy on those who have died.

o: Aisha's arrival in his household in Medina
the year Quraysh drove his family out of Mecca
the loss of the wife he never stopped mentioning

p: a voice at the door like her sister's
good news of a house in Paradise

s: she says she never saw her; she knew her through how often he spoke of her.
he sent meat to Khadijah's friends after her death
Aisha reports it in Sahih al-Bukhari.
in Sahih Muslim he says he was given her love
love described as a gift, not an achievement.

games.q: you're in his house years later. a woman at the door asks to come in, and her voice sounds like someone long gone. what happens?
o: he's shaken, and calls out Hala's name.
he asks her to come back another day.
games.why: Bukhari reports that Hala's way of asking reminded him of Khadijah; he was shaken, and said: O Allah, Hala.

practice: Bring to mind one person who is gone, and let one ordinary detail come back: a voice, a phrase they used, a dish they made, the way they knocked.

If you can, say their name quietly, and one thing they did that you're glad of; if you pray, you can ask Allah's mercy for them, the way Muslims do for those who have died. If it's too heavy today, just their name is enough.

wordCard.voice: Khadijah dies. And in the hadith, she is still in his speech long after: her friends fed, her sister's voice recognized, her love called a gift. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the name of the Prophet's wife Khadijah bint Khuwaylid.

carryVoice: Your line: he never forgot her. In the hadith, that kind of love is a gift. Day seven hundred forty-eight.
